newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress party starts vote-counting.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress party starts vote-counting.

text.p: India's Congress party on Thursday began counting votes in a rare internal election that its president Sitaram Kesri was widely expected to win.

Dozens of policemen and paramilitary soldiers stood guard outside the party's office in leafy central Delhi to prevent any disruptions. Party officials said results were expected only after 4 p.m. (1030 GMT).
Supporters of Kesri, dressed in the white handspun cotton clothes traditionally worn by Indian politicians, shouted slogans outside the gates and clamoured to be allowed inside.
The poll, held on Monday, was only the third election in the 112-year history of India's oldest political party, traditionally dominated by charismatic leaders.

Once the driving force behind the movement against colonial rule, Congress has ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947, with former prime ministers Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi in power for 37 years.
The party of Mahatma Gandhi suffered a crushing defeat in general elections last year after more than half a dozen ministers resigned in connection with a money-laundering scandal.
Kesri, a follower of Mahatma Gandhi, assumed the party presidency last September when former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned in disgrace over another corruption scandal.
Congress was forced to hold the internal poll after the Election Commission declared it would recognise only those parties which democratically elect their leaders by mid-June.
More than 8,000 Congress activists across India took part.
Analysts said the shrewd 76-year-old Kesri was likely to sweep aside opposition from two younger challengers, who say new blood is essential to rejuvenate the once mighty party.

Congress still wields considerable power through the vital support it extends to prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-party coalition government in parliament. The centre-left coalition controls 179 seats in India's 543-member lower house, where it is supported by Congress's 140 deputies.
In March, Congress suddenly withdrew its backing to Gujral's predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, and later toppled him in a parliamentary confidence vote.

Gujral's party, the Janata Dal, is due to hold internal elections next week. The group's president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, has been linked to a scandal over animal fodder funds, and the party is deeply divided between his supporters and critics.
